# Effect of In-Hospital Initiation of Dapagliflozin on Decongestion in Patients Hospitalized for Heart Failure

# An Analysis of the DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68 Trial

Andre M. Small, MD, a Siddharth M. Patel, MD, MPH, b,c Colleen Thomas, MS, b,c Michael G. Palazzolo, MS, b,c

Jan B  elohlávek, MD, PHD, d,e Akshay S. Desai, MD, MPH, c Jarosław Dro _ zd _ z, MD, PHD, f Silvio E. Inzucchi, MD, g

John J.V. McMurray, MD, h Béla Merkely, MD, PHD, i Eileen O’Meara, MD, j Subodh Verma, MD, PHD, k

Stephen D. Wiviott, MD, l Marc S. Sabatine, MD, MPH, b,c David D. Berg, MD, MPH b,c

## ABSTRACT

BACKGROUND Safe and effective decongestion remains an important therapeutic goal in patients hospitalized for

heart failure.

OBJECTIVES The authors evaluated the effect of dapagliflozin on multiple clinically relevant measures of congestion

among patients hospitalized for heart failure.

METHODS This was a prespecified analysis of DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68 (Dapagliflozin Effect on Cardiovascular Events in

Acute Heart Failure—Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction 68), a randomized, placebo-controlled trial evaluating in-

hospital initiation of dapagliflozin on clinical outcomes through 2 months. The authors assessed placebo-adjusted

changes from baseline in modified EVEREST (Efficacy of Vasopressin Antagonism in Heart Failure) Composite Congestion

Score (CCS), body weight, mean daily loop diuretic dose (furosemide 40 mg intravenous [IV] equivalents), and body

weight adjusted for mean daily loop diuretic dose (diuretic efficiency) at 1 week, 1 month, and 2 months using linear

mixed-effects models for repeated measures.

RESULTS At randomization, 12%, 63%, and 24% had no congestion (CCS 0), mild-to-moderate congestion (CCS 1-3),

and severe congestion (CCS 4-9), respectively. Compared with placebo, dapagliflozin improved all decongestion-related

endpoints by 1 week, including CCS (least squares mean difference [LSMD]: − 0.18; 95% CI: − 0.33 to − 0.04; P = 0.011),

body weight (LSMD: − 0.60 kg; 95% CI: − 0.95 to − 0.26; P < 0.001), mean daily loop diuretic dose (LSMD: − 0.12

furosemide 40-mg IV equivalents; 95% CI: − 0.22 to − 0.02; P = 0.014), and diuretic efficiency (LSMD: − 0.93 kg/

furosemide 40 mg IV equivalents; 95% CI: − 1.61 to − 0.25; P = 0.008). These improvements were sustained through

2 months, with progressive increases in diuretic efficiency through 2 months (LSMD: − 1.99 kg/furosemide 40 mg IV

equivalents; 95% CI: − 3.19 to − 0.78; P < 0.001).

CONCLUSIONS In-hospital initiation of dapagliflozin led to modest but significant improvements across multiple mea-

sures of congestion within 1 week that were sustained through 2 months. Diuretic efficiency progressively improved through

2 months. (Dapagliflozin Effect on Cardiovascular Events in Acute Heart Failure—Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction 68

## H

eart failure (HF) hospitalizations

are associated with a high risk of

death and other adverse outcomes

during hospital admission and in the early

postdischarge period, with congestion

serving as a key pathophysiological and

clinical feature. 1 Despite the use of loop di-

uretics, residual congestion at discharge is

common and strongly associated with HF

readmission and mortality. These observa-

tions have motivated interest in therapies

that more effectively promote decongestion

during hospitalization and in the early post-

discharge period. 2-5

Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) in-

hibitors, such as dapagliflozin, are a foundational

component of guideline-directed pharmacological

therapy for HF across the spectrum of left ventricular

ejection fraction (LVEF), with randomized trials

demonstrating robust reductions in the risk of wors-

ening heart failure (WHF) and cardiovascular death

(CVD) in ambulatory patients with HF. 6,7 In addition,

the totality of randomized trial data suggests that in-

hospital initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors reduces the

early risk of CVD or WHF and of all-cause mortality in

the early postdischarge period in hospitalized pa-

tients with HF. 8,9 Beyond their established clinical

benefits, SGLT2 inhibitors may have favorable early

effects on fluid balance through mechanisms that

include osmotic diuresis, natriuresis, and facilitation

of interstitial drainage. 10 These effects may be

particularly advantageous in the management of

decompensated HF, uniquely positioning SGLT2 in-

hibitors to achieve the dual goals of effective decon-

gestion and durable cardiovascular risk reduction.

Despite the theoretical benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors

on decongestion, studies evaluating the impact of

in-hospital initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors on

decongestion-related endpoints have produced

mixed results. 11-13 DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68 (Dapagli-

flozin Effect on Cardiovascular Events in Acute Heart

Failure-Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction 68;

NCT04363697) was a randomized, placebo-controlled

trial evaluating in-hospital initiation of dapagliflozin

on clinical outcomes through 2 months in patients

hospitalized with a primary diagnosis of HF. 8 In this

prespecified secondary analysis of DAPA ACT HF-

TIMI 68, we evaluated the effect of in-hospital initi-

ation of dapagliflozin on multiple decongestion-

related endpoints in the early postdischarge period.

## METHODS

STUDY POPULATION. The DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68

trial design, baseline characteristics, and main

results have previously been published. 8,14 In brief,

DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68 was a randomized, double-

blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluating the

efficacy and safety of in-hospital initiation of dapa-

gliflozin in 2,401 patients hospitalized for HF.

Eligible patients were at least 18 years old and had a

primary diagnosis of HF, including signs and symp-

toms of fluid overload with elevated natriuretic

peptide levels. Randomization occurred during the

index hospitalization, at least 24 hours and no later

than 14 days after hospital admission, and as early as

possible after initial clinical stabilization. Stabiliza-

tion criteria included no intensification in the dose of

intravenous (IV) diuretics during the 12 hours before

randomization and no use of IV vasodilators or ino-

tropes during the 24 hours before randomization.

Patients were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive

dapagliflozin (10 mg once daily) or matching placebo

and were followed for clinical outcomes through

2 months. The trial protocol was approved by the

institutional review board or ethics committee at

each participating site and all participants provided

written informed consent before enrollment.

DECONGESTION-RELATED ENDPOINTS. The primary

decongestion-related endpoint for this analysis was

the placebo-adjusted change from baseline in modi-

fied EVEREST (Efficacy of Vasopressin Antagonism in

Heart Failure) Composite Congestion Score (CCS). 2

Six HF signs and symptoms—orthopnea, peripheral

edema, jugular venous pressure (JVP), rales, fatigue,

and dyspnea—were graded on a scale from 0 (absent)

to 3 (severe) at randomization, 1 week, 1 month, and

2 months. Modified CCS was calculated by summing

the individual component scores for orthopnea, pe-

ripheral edema, and JVP (maximum score = 9 points).

In the prespecified primary analysis, placebo-

adjusted change from baseline in CCS was analyzed

using a complete-case approach, restricting to pa-

tients with evaluable scores (ie, available scores for

all 3 CCS components) at both baseline and the rele-

vant follow-up visit. Sensitivity analyses were per-

formed using multiple imputation methods to handle

missing CCS data. In addition, placebo-adjusted

change from baseline was assessed for each individ-

ual HF sign and symptom. Full details are provided in

the Supplemental Methods.

Other decongestion-related endpoints included

placebo-adjusted change from baseline in body

weight, placebo-adjusted change from baseline in

mean daily loop diuretic dose (expressed as furose-

mide 40 mg IV equivalents), and placebo-adjusted

change from baseline in body weight adjusted for

mean daily loop diuretic dose, with greater weight loss

per unit of loop diuretic defining greater diuretic effi-

ciency. Analyses of body weight and diuretic effi-

ciency excluded observations of change in body

weight below the first and above the 99th percentiles

to mitigate against the impact of extreme outliers.

Loop diuretic equivalence is shown in the

Supplemental Methods. Analysis of these endpoints

was similarly restricted to patients with evaluable data

at both baseline and the relevant follow-up visit. No

imputation methods were used for these endpoints.

CLINICAL ENDPOINTS. The primary clinical endpoint

in DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68 was the composite of CVD/

WHF through 2 months. A WHF event was defined as:

1) worsening of signs or symptoms of HF during the

index hospitalization, resulting in treatment with IV

inotropes, mechanical circulatory support, invasive

ventilatory support, or heart transplantation; 2) un-

planned rehospitalization for HF; or 3) urgent

ambulatory HF visit resulting in treatment with IV

diuretic therapy. Secondary clinical endpoints

included each individual component of the primary

clinical endpoint, cardiovascular death or rehospi-

talization for HF, and all-cause death.

STATISTICAL ANALYSES. Patients were classified as

having no congestion (CCS 0), mild-to-moderate

congestion (CCS 1-3), or severe congestion (CCS 4-9)

at the time of randomization. The threshold between

mild-to-moderate and severe congestion was derived

based on maximizing the Youden index applied to a

time-dependent receiver operating characteristic

curve at 60 days postrandomization for the primary

clinical endpoint because there are no well-

established thresholds for assessing severity of re-

sidual congestion during HF hospitalization rather

than at the time of discharge. 15,16 Baseline charac-

teristics were summarized according to baseline

congestion severity using counts and percentages for

categorical variables and medians (Q1-Q3) for

continuous variables. Trends across congestion strata

were assessed using the Jonckheere-Terpstra test for

ordinal and continuous variables and the Cochran-

Armitage trend test for binary variables.

The associations of congestion parameters at

randomization, including CCS and individual HF

signs and symptoms, with time-to-event clinical

endpoints were evaluated using multivariable Cox

proportional hazards models adjusted for age, esti-

mated glomerular filtration rate, LVEF, previous HF

hospitalization, previous stroke, atrial fibrillation,

use of invasive or noninvasive ventilation before

randomization, and randomized treatment. Adjusted

HRs (aHRs) and corresponding 95% CIs were esti-

mated per 2-point increase in CCS (corresponding

approximately to 1 SD). P values (Wald test) were

obtained from the Cox model. The proportional

hazards assumption was confirmed using scaled

Schoenfeld residual plots. Owing to inconclusive

evidence regarding the linearity assumption for the

relationship between CCS and the log-hazard for the

primary clinical endpoint, aHRs also were estimated

for CCS categories with uncongested (CCS = 0) as the

reference group. Firth’s correction was used when a

congestion category did not have any events for a

given endpoint. Adjusted cumulative risk curves for

time-to-event clinical endpoints by CCS category

were derived from a multivariable Cox model using

direct standardization to the covariate distribution in

our cohort with evaluable CCS.

The effect of dapagliflozin on changes in CCS over

time was analyzed using a linear mixed model for

repeated measures, including all eligible postbase-

line visits, with fixed effects for baseline CCS,

randomization stratification factors (HF chronicity

and type 2 diabetes), randomized treatment assign-

ment (dapagliflozin or placebo), visit (week 1, month

1, and month 2), and interaction of treatment and

visit with an unstructured covariance matrix to

account for correlation among visits. Results are re-

ported as least squares mean changes and placebo-

adjusted least squares mean differences (LSMDs)

with 95% CIs at each postrandomization study visit.

Similar linear mixed-effects models were used to

assess placebo-adjusted change in body weight,

placebo-adjusted change in mean daily loop diuretic

dose, and placebo-adjusted change in body weight

per mean daily loop diuretic dose. The effects of

dapagliflozin on congestion-related endpoints were

evaluated in subgroups defined by baseline LVEF

(#40% vs >40%) and baseline loop diuretic dose

(<40 vs $40 mg/day IV furosemide equivalents).

The comparative treatment effects of dapagliflozin

vs placebo on time-to-event clinical outcomes were

assessed according to baseline CCS by including

terms for randomized treatment, baseline CCS cate-

gory, and a randomized treatment-by-CCS category

interaction term in each stratified Cox model. Het-

erogeneity of treatment effect across baseline CCS

categories was evaluated based on the type III Wald P

value for the interaction of randomized treatment

assignment and CCS category.

All P values and 95% CIs are 2-sided without

adjustment for multiple testing. R version 4.5.3 was

used to estimate the Youden index (cenROC package

version 2.0.0) and estimate covariate-adjusted cu-

mulative risk curves (adjustedCurves package

version 0.11.4). SAS version 9.4 was used for all other

analyses.

## RESULTS

DISTRIBUTION OF BASELINE CONGESTION

PARAMETERS. Among 2,401 randomized trial par-

ticipants, 1,676 patients had complete baseline CCS

data and were included in the primary CCS analyses.

Baseline characteristics of patients with vs without

complete baseline CCS data are shown in

Supplemental Table 1. Among patients with complete

baseline CCS data, complete follow-up CCS data were

available in 1,154 (68.9%) at week 1, 1,253 (74.8%) at

month 1, and 1,165 (69.5%) at month 2. At randomi-

zation, the median CCS was 2 (Q1-Q3: 1-3), with

12.2%, 63.3%, and 24.5% classified as uncongested

(CCS 0), mild-to-moderately congested (CCS 1-3), and

severely congested (CCS 4-9), respectively. Irre-

spective of randomized treatment, CCS scores tended

to decrease over time, with median CCS scores of

2 (Q1-Q3: 1-3), 1 (Q1-Q3: 1-2), 1 (Q1-Q3: 0-2), and 1

(Q1-Q3: 0-1) at randomization, week 1, month 1, and

month 2, respectively (Supplemental Table 2,

Supplemental Figure 1).

BASELINE CHARACTERISTICS OF STUDY

POPULATION. Baseline characteristics are presented

by baseline CCS in Table 1. Age, sex, and LVEF were

similar across congestion categories. Patients in

higher congestion categories were more likely to be

Black, and to have a higher body mass index, type 2

diabetes mellitus, and estimated glomerular filtration

rate <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Patients in higher conges-

tion categories were also more likely to have chronic

HF and at least 1 previous HF hospitalization. Greater

congestion severity was associated with lower Kan-

sas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores

(reflecting poorer health status) and higher natri-

uretic peptide levels. Median baseline body weight

was 82.0 kg (Q1-Q3: 69.0-96.7 kg), 84.4 kg (Q1-Q3:

71.1-101.6 kg), and 96.2 kg (Q1-Q3: 79.1-113.7 kg)

among patients with CCS 0, CCS 1 to 3, and CCS 4 to

9, respectively.

PROGNOSTIC SIGNIFICANCE OF CONGESTION

VARIABLES AND EVEREST CCS. Event rates

increased in a graded fashion across increasing

congestion categories for all primary and secondary

clinical endpoints (Figure 1). Baseline congestion

severity was independently associated with pro-

gressively higher risk of each clinical endpoint

through 2 months (Figure 2). For the primary clinical

endpoint of CVD or WHF, aHRs increased from 1.97

(95% CI: 1.12-3.49) for CCS 1-3 to 2.23 (95% CI: 1.22-

4.07) for CCS 4-9 compared with CCS 0. A similar

gradient was observed for all-cause death (aHR: 1.95;

95% CI: 0.59-6.39 and aHR: 3.60; 95% CI: 1.08-12.0,

respectively). Baseline congestion severity did not

appear to modify the effect of dapagliflozin on clin-

ical outcomes (Supplemental Figure 2).

Among individual HF signs and symptoms, in

adjusted analyses, severity of peripheral edema was

independently associated with the risks of both CVD

or WHF (P trend = 0.008) and all-cause death

(P trend < 0.001). Severity of JVP elevation was

independently associated with risk of all-cause death

(P trend = 0.027), and severity of orthopnea was

independently associated with risk of CVD or WHF

(P trend = 0.010). By contrast, severity of dyspnea,

fatigue, and rales was not independently associated

with either of these short-term morbidity and mor-

tality outcomes (Supplemental Table 3).

EFFECT OF DAPAGLIFLOZIN ON EVEREST

CCS. Compared with placebo, dapagliflozin signifi-

cantly albeit modestly reduced CCS at 1 week

(LSMD: − 0.18; 95% CI: − 0.33 to − 0.04; P = 0.011),

with sustained effects at 1 month (LSMD: − 0.16;

EFFECT OF DAPAGLIFLOZIN ON BODY WEIGHT,

MEAN DAILY DIURETIC DOSE, AND DIURETIC

EFFICIENCY. Compared with placebo, dapagliflozin

led to a significantly greater reduction in body weight

at 1 week (LSMD: − 0.60 kg; 95% CI: − 0.95 to − 0.26;

P < 0.001), with sustained reductions at 1 month

(LSMD: − 0.84 kg; 95% CI: − 1.27 to − 0.41; P < 0.001)

and 2 months (LSMD: − 0.74 kg; 95% CI: − 1.21

to − 0.26; P = 0.002) (Figure 3B).

Mean daily loop diuretic dose decreased from

baseline in both treatment groups at all follow-up

visits. Compared with placebo, reductions were

significantly greater with dapagliflozin at 1 week

(LSMD: − 0.12 furosemide 40 mg IV equivalents;

95% CI: − 0.22 to − 0.02; P = 0.014), with progres-

sively greater reductions at 1 month (LSMD: − 0.15

SUBGROUP ANALYSES. The treatment effect of

dapagliflozin vs placebo on congestion-related

endpoints appeared generally consistent irre-

## DISCUSSION

In this prespecified analysis of DAPA ACT HF-TIMI

68, we evaluated the effect of in-hospital initiation

of dapagliflozin on decongestion-related parameters

during the early postdischarge period among patients

hospitalized for HF. Several key findings emerged.

First, greater baseline congestion was independently

associated with higher risks of HF-related events and

death through 2 months. Second, dapagliflozin led to

modest but significant improvements across multiple

complementary measures of congestion, with treat-

ment effects evident by 1 week after randomization

and sustained through 2 months. Third, diuretic ef-

ficiency progressively improved over time with

dapagliflozin, reflecting sustained weight loss and

reduced background loop diuretic requirements.

Collectively, these findings demonstrate that

in-hospital initiation of dapagliflozin during HF

remains the principal reason for HF hospitalization

and one of the strongest predictors of adverse out-

dently associated with higher risk of WHF events,

findings are consistent with previous analyses from

demonstrating that residual congestion is a major

predictor of postdischarge risk. 3,5,19 Notably, in our

study from a large contemporary clinical trial cohort,

objective physical signs of congestion—including

peripheral edema, elevated JVP, and orthopnea—

were more strongly associated with adverse out-

comes than patient-reported symptoms such as dys-

pnea and fatigue. These observations reinforce the

continued value of bedside congestion assessment

EFFECTS OF DAPAGLIFLOZIN ON DECONGESTION-

RELATED ENDPOINTS. Dapagliflozin favorably

affected multiple complementary measures of

congestion within 1 week of treatment initiation.

This temporal pattern is consistent with the known

natriuretic and osmotic diuretic effects of SGLT2 in-

hibitors. Interestingly, diuretic efficiency, a widely

recognized marker of decongestive efficacy,

continued to improve over time, driven by reduced

loop diuretic requirements. If these benefits were

mediated exclusively through early natriuresis and

osmotic diuresis, one would not expect these curves

to continue to diverge, particularly because the early

diuretic response is known to be rapidly offset by

increased water reabsorption in the more distal

segments of the nephron. 20 Instead, the pattern

observed in our study suggests that the sustained

favorable effects of dapagliflozin on congestion pa-

rameters may be related to effects beyond direct

diuretic augmentation.

Several mechanisms may contribute to this

observation. Experimental and clinical studies sug-

gest that SGLT2 inhibitors promote preferential

mobilization of interstitial fluid while preserving

intravascular volume, a profile that differs from

conventional loop diuretics. 21,22 SGLT2 inhibitors

have also been shown to restore tubuloglomerular

feedback, improve ventricular geometry and reduce

cardiac filling pressures, and modulate neurohor-

monal pathways that contribute to sodium and water

retention. 23,24 Whether these sustained improve-

ments reflect improved responsiveness to conven-

tional diuretic therapy or other disease-modifying

inhibitors in patients hospitalized for HF. In EMPA-

RELATIONSHIP TO CLINICAL OUTCOMES. Although

dapagliflozin did not significantly reduce the primary

composite endpoint of CVD or WHF through 60 days

in DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68, the totality of randomized

trial data based on a meta-analysis of SOLOIST-WHF

(Effect of Sotagliflozin on Cardiovascular Events in

Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Post Worsening

Heart Failure), EMPULSE, and DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68,

suggests that in-hospital initiation of SGLT2 in-

hibitors reduces the high risk of clinical events,

including all-cause mortality, in the early post-

discharge period. 8 Importantly, there was no evi-

dence that baseline congestion severity modified the

treatment effect of dapagliflozin on clinical out-

comes. These findings suggest that although

congestion identifies risk, it does not identify pa-

tients who preferentially benefit from SGLT2 in-

hibitors. Accordingly, congestion severity should not

be used to guide decisions regarding initiation of

SGLT2 inhibitors among otherwise eligible hospital-

ized patients.

CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS. HF hospitalization repre-

sents a critical opportunity to initiate evidence-

based HF therapies. Our findings demonstrate that

initiation of dapagliflozin after clinical stabilization

leads to early improvements across complementary

measures of congestion that persist through the

vulnerable postdischarge period. Together with the

established safety profile of in-hospital initiation of

SGLT2 inhibitors, these findings provide additional

support for implementation of SGLT2 inhibitors

during HF hospitalization rather than deferring

treatment until after discharge.

STUDY LIMITATIONS. First, congestion was assessed

using a CCS that relies on clinical assessment of signs

and symptoms. Although sites were prospectively

trained on the assessment of HF signs and symptoms,

and data were recorded on dedicated pages in the

electronic case report form (eCRF), the scoring sys-

tem can be subjective. Moreover, because the specific

study staff members performing the assessments

were not recorded in the eCRF and replicate assess-

ments by multiple observers were not required, we

are not able to formally assess interobserver reli-

ability. Second, some patients had missing conges-

tion data; however, multiple imputation methods

yielded treatment effects that were directionally

consistent with the primary analysis. Third, change

in body weight is an imperfect surrogate for fluid loss

in patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors, because

SGLT2 inhibitors produce a net calorie deficit by

increasing glycosuria. However, the concurrent

reduction in loop diuretic dosing with dapagliflozin

supports the interpretation that the observed weight

loss is related to a decongestive effect. Fourth,

additional measures of decongestion, including bio-

markers, urine output, and invasive hemodynamics,

were not available and may have provided additional

mechanistic insight. Fifth, there was no adjustment

made for multiple comparisons; thus, the possibility

of chance findings among the multiple decongestion-

related endpoints and time points cannot be

excluded. Finally, follow-up was limited to 2 months,

precluding assessment of longer-term relationships

between changes in congestion parameters and clin-

ical outcomes. However, this study period encom-

passes the time period during which the

decongestive effects of SGLT2 inhibitors would be

expected to emerge and therefore is particularly

relevant to the objectives of this analysis.

## CONCLUSIONS

Among patients hospitalized for HF in DAPA ACT

HF-TIMI 68, greater baseline congestion identified

patients at higher risk of HF-related events and

death, reinforcing the potential value of therapies

that promote decongestion during hospitalization

and in the early postdischarge period. In-hospital

initiation of dapagliflozin led to improvements in

multiple clinically relevant measures of congestion

within 1 week of treatment initiation, with progres-

sive improvements in diuretic efficiency through

2 months. Although the temporal pattern of these

effects may not be attributable solely to direct

diuretic actions, the mechanisms underlying the

sustained decongestive effects cannot be determined

from this analysis. These findings provide further

insight into the role of SGLT2 inhibitors in patients

hospitalized for HF and support in-hospital initiation

of dapagliflozin following clinical stabilization.
